cards.a: CBWFQ (Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing) gives each class a guaranteed bandwidth share, while LLQ (Low Latency Queuing) adds a strict-priority class, typically voice EF, served before all others but rate-limited so it cannot starve other classes.
CBWFQ matches traffic into classes and gives each class a guaranteed bandwidth share with the bandwidth command, serving packets proportionally to each class's weight.

cards.q: What does the priority command do in LLQ?
cards.a: The priority command creates a strict-priority LLQ class that is served first and is policed to the configured rate so it cannot monopolize the link and starve other classes.

cards.q: What is the difference between priority and bandwidth commands?
cards.a: priority defines a strict-priority, policed LLQ class, while bandwidth defines a guaranteed weighted CBWFQ share that is not strict-priority.

cards.q: Why must the LLQ priority class be policed?
cards.a: A strict-priority queue would otherwise consume the entire link and starve all lower-priority classes; policing it to the configured priority value guarantees other classes still get service.

cards.q: Which traffic is typically placed in the LLQ priority class?
cards.a: Voice traffic marked EF is typically placed in the LLQ priority class because it is latency and jitter sensitive.

cards.q: What does queue-limit do in CBWFQ?
cards.a: queue-limit sets the per-class queue depth, controlling how many packets can buffer before tail-drop occurs for that class.

cards.q: Voice traffic jitters on a congested WAN link; what is the likely fix?
cards.a: Add an LLQ priority class for the voice EF traffic so it is served before other classes and not queued behind data.

cards.q: What happens if the LLQ priority value is configured too high?
cards.a: Other classes can be starved of bandwidth because the priority queue is served first; LLQ's priority class must be appropriately limited.

cards.q: What is the LLQ and CBWFQ quick-review summary?
cards.a: CBWFQ guarantees per-class bandwidth while LLQ adds a strict, policed priority class for voice EF, so use priority for latency-sensitive traffic and bandwidth for video/data to keep voice jitter-free without starving other classes.
